---
title: "Line charts"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
gbp <- scales::label_dollar(prefix = "£", scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")
```

The examples follow the visualisation team's Storybook, on its demo data,
and carry the full set of labels a published chart does: a title that states
the finding, a subtitle that names the measure and the period, a source, a
note and a byline.

## Single line

A 2px `data-primary` line. The value axis has no title; the subtitle names
the unit. The baseline is drawn when the axis starts at zero.

```{r single}
a <- gla_monthly[gla_monthly$series == "Variable A", ]

p <- ggplot(a, aes(month, value)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  gla_zero_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "In London, Variable A's value has fallen steadily since 2017",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP), January 2015 to March 2024",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", note = "Data for demonstration only",
    byline = "GLA City Intelligence", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
p
```

Every chart should carry a text alternative. `gla_describe()` writes one
from the plot and `gla_alt()` sets it; a better one says what the chart
shows.

```{r alt}
gla_describe(p)
```

## Multiple lines

Series are named at the end of the line, with a marker on the last point,
rather than in a legend. Labels that would overlap are pushed apart. Leave
room on the right with the x expansion.

```{r multiple}
ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endpoint() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = series)) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.18))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(
    title = "All three variables have converged since 2020",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP), January 2015 to March 2024",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", byline = "GLA City Intelligence", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## Dual line

Two series where one is the subject and the other the reference: the
`auto` scale colours London in primary and the comparator in context grey.
Draw the reference first so the subject sits on top.

```{r dual}
d <- gla_monthly[gla_monthly$series != "Variable C", ]
d$series <- ifelse(d$series == "Variable A", "London", "England")
d <- d[order(d$series == "London"), ]

ggplot(d, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = series)) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(
    title = "London has tracked England since 2020",
    subtitle = "Monthly estimated variable value (GBP)",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## Reference line and range

A target or an average is a dashed rule in context grey with its label on
the line. A period is a wash behind the data.

```{r reference}
ggplot(a, aes(month, value)) +
  annotate_gla_range(xmin = as.Date("2020-03-01"), xmax = as.Date("2021-07-01")) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  gla_reference_line(mean(a$value), "Average") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Variable A was below its average through the pandemic",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP); the shaded period is March 2020 to June 2021",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
```

## Forecast

A projection is drawn the way the web charts draw one: the line goes
dashed from the point the projection starts, and the period carries a
`data-context` wash, a dashed rule and the word "Projected". The line is
solid up to the point and dashed from it, meeting there, so it does not
break. `geom_gla_line(projected_from = )` draws the line and
`annotate_gla_projection()` the period; both take a date on a date axis.

```{r forecast}
actual <- gla_monthly[gla_monthly$series == "Variable A" & gla_monthly$month < as.Date("2023-01-01"), ]
last <- actual[nrow(actual), ]
projected <- data.frame(
  month = seq(last$month, by = "month", length.out = 16)[-1],
  series = "Variable A",
  value = last$value * cumprod(rep(0.995, 15))
)
a_forecast <- rbind(actual, projected)

ggplot(a_forecast, aes(month, value)) +
  annotate_gla_projection(from = last$month) +
  geom_gla_line(projected_from = last$month) +
  geom_gla_endpoint() +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Variable A is projected to keep falling through 2024",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP); from December 2022 the values are projected",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", note = "Projection for demonstration only", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
```

## Line styles

When a chart carries a second dimension that colour cannot, the web
charts dash it: solid for the first set of lines, dashed for the second.
Here each series is a colour and the measure against its twelve-month
average is the style. `scale_linetype_gla()` maps the set; the legend
names the styles and the lines are labelled by series.

```{r styles}
ab <- gla_monthly[gla_monthly$series %in% c("Variable A", "Variable B"), ]
ab <- ab[order(ab$series, ab$month), ]
ab$average <- ave(ab$value, ab$series, FUN = function(v) stats::filter(v, rep(1 / 12, 12), sides = 1))
styled <- rbind(
  data.frame(month = ab$month, series = ab$series, value = ab$average, kind = "12-month average"),
  data.frame(month = ab$month, series = ab$series, value = ab$value, kind = "Monthly")
)
styled <- styled[!is.na(styled$value) & styled$month >= as.Date("2021-01-01"), ]

ggplot(styled, aes(month, value, colour = series, linetype = kind)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = series), data = styled[styled$kind == "12-month average", ]) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla(guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_gla() +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Both variables sit below their twelve-month average in 2024",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP) and its trailing twelve-month average, 2021 to 2024",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
```

## Area

An area is the line's fill at a fifth opacity, with the line drawn over it.

```{r area}
ggplot(a, aes(month, value)) +
  geom_gla_area() +
  geom_gla_line() +
  gla_zero_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Variable A", subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP)",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
```

## Faceted

One panel per series, stacked, each with its own axes and the series name
as its heading: `facet_gla_rows()`. The Small multiples article covers
shared against free scales.

```{r facets, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  facet_gla_rows(vars(series)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Each variable on its own", subtitle = "Monthly value, GBP", x = NULL) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## Dark

A chart for an inverse surface. `gla_mode("dark")` switches every function
at once: the theme, the scales, the reference line, the range, the
projection and the map boundaries all read their colours from the dark
tokens, so nothing is left in light-mode grey. `with_gla_mode()` does it for
one chart in a light document, as here.

```{r dark}
with_gla_mode("dark", {
  ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
    geom_gla_line() +
    geom_gla_endpoint() +
    geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = series)) +
    gla_reference_line(30000, "Target") +
    scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.18))) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
    scale_colour_gla() +
    gla_labs(
      title = "All three variables have converged since 2020",
      subtitle = "London monthly estimated variable value (GBP)",
      source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL
    ) +
    theme_gla(legend = "none")
})
```

Every function still takes `theme = "dark"` directly, which wins over the
mode for that one call.
